title: Local Variables (part 2 of 2): IMUL, MOVZX/MOVSX, Array and Struct Locals

questions.q: The single-operand instruction `imul r/m32` multiplies its operand by which register, and where does the product go?
choices: By EAX; the 64-bit product goes into EDX:EAX (EDX = high half)
By EAX; the product is truncated into EAX
By EDX; the product goes into EAX:EDX (EAX = high half)
By itself; the result overwrites the operand
questions.explain: One-operand IMUL uses implicit registers: EDX:EAX = EAX * r/m32. The output is twice the input width, so nothing is truncated.

questions.q: `imul r/m8` (one 8-bit operand) performs which operation?
questions.explain: The 8-bit one-operand form multiplies AL by the byte operand and writes the 16-bit product to AX. DX is used only by the larger one-operand forms (DX:AX, EDX:EAX, RDX:RAX).

questions.q: Which of these IMUL forms can lose the high bits of the product (truncation)?
questions.explain: One-operand forms store a double-width result (DX:AX ... RDX:RAX), so they can't truncate. Two- and three-operand forms store into a register the same size as the inputs, so a large product gets cut off.

questions.q: IMUL has a three-operand form that encodes a full 64-bit immediate, e.g. `imul r64, r/m64, imm64`.
questions.explain: The largest immediate is 32 bits. `imul r64, r/m64, imm32` sign-extends the imm32 to 64 bits. In the debugger, the instruction bytes hold only 4 bytes of immediate.

questions.q: In `imul r64, r/m64, imm32`, how is the 32-bit immediate used?
choices: It is sign-extended to 64 bits, then multiplied by r/m64
It is zero-extended to 64 bits, then multiplied by r/m64
It is multiplied by only the low 32 bits of r/m64
It is placed in the upper 32 bits of a 64-bit constant
questions.explain: r64 = r/m64 * sign-extended imm32. A negative imm32 stays negative after it is widened to 64 bits.

questions.q: Which three-operand IMUL form takes a 16-bit immediate?
choices: All of the r16, r32 and r64 forms
questions.explain: There's just one imm16 form, and its result is 16 bits, so truncation is possible. The 32- and 64-bit three-operand forms take either an imm8 (sign-extended) or an imm32.

questions.q: For the three-operand form `imul reg, r/mX, imm`, which statements are true?
choices: The first operand (destination) must be a register
The second operand can be a register or a memory location
The destination's previous value is one of the numbers multiplied
questions.explain: reg = r/mX * imm. The destination is only written: in `imul r12, rax, 12341234h`, the old R12 value (0x84) played no part.

questions.q: In `imul r32, r/m32, imm8`, the immediate byte is 0xFF. What multiplier does it represent?
questions.explain: In the imm8 forms, the immediate is sign-extended to the operand size. 0xFF has its top bit set, so it becomes 0xFFFFFFFF = -1, and the instruction negates r/m32.

questions.q: Visual Studio tends to emit signed `imul` even where unsigned `mul` would be expected, for example when multiplying unsigned values.
questions.explain: VS strongly prefers imul. The author couldn't get it to emit plain mul for simple examples. Seeing imul where mul would fit can hint that the code was built with VS.

questions.q: What is the signed (two's complement) decimal value of the byte 0x84?
questions.explain: The top bit is set, so the value is negative. 0x100 - 0x84 = 0x7C = 124, so 0x84 = -124.

questions.q: RAX = 0x609966C1A977E177 and R12 = 0x84. After `imul r12b`, what hex value is in AX?
questions.explain: AX = AL * r12b. AL = 0x77 = +119, and r12b = 0x84 = -124. 119 * -124 = -14756 = -0x39A4. As a 16-bit two's complement value that is 0x10000 - 0x39A4 = 0xC65C.

questions.q: Same starting registers (RAX = 0x609966C1A977E177, R12 = 0x84). What is the full RAX after `imul r12b`?
questions.explain: The 8-bit one-operand form writes only AX. The other 48 bits of RAX are unchanged.

questions.q: With R12 = 0x84, why is the operand negative in `imul r12b` but +132 in `imul r12d, eax`?
choices: As a byte, 0x84 has its top bit set; as a dword, 0x00000084 has a top bit of 0
imul treats register operands as negative and memory operands as positive
The r12d form zero-extends R12 first, while the r12b form sign-extends it
0x84 is always negative; the sign of the product just happens to cancel
questions.explain: Whether a value is negative depends on the operand size. Check the most significant bit at that width: bit 7 of 0x84 is 1, but bit 31 of 0x00000084 is 0.

questions.q: R12 = 0x84 and RAX = 0x609966C1A977E177. What is R12 after `imul r12d, eax`?
questions.explain: r12d = r12d * eax. EAX = 0xA977E177 is negative (top bit set) and r12d = +132, so the true product is negative. Only its low 32 bits are kept: 0x61D0415C. 0x5761D0415C is the full unsigned product, which a 32-bit destination can't hold. In the example, the upper half of R12 ends up 0.

questions.q: R12 = 0x84 and RAX = 0x609966C1A977E177. What does `imul r12, rax, 12341234h` compute?
choices: RAX * 0x0000000012341234 (the imm32 sign-extended), with the result in R12
R12 * RAX * 0x12341234, with the result in R12
R12 * 0x12341234, with the result in RAX
EAX * 0x12341234, with the result in R12D
questions.explain: Three-operand form: r64 = r/m64 * sign-extended imm32. The old R12 value is never used. 0x12341234 is positive, so sign extension just adds zeros. R12 ends up as 0xE5A3577504602A2C.

questions.q: AL = 0x02 and BL = 0xFF. After `imul bl`, what hex value is in AX?
questions.explain: In a signed multiply, BL = 0xFF = -1, so AX = 2 * -1 = -2 = 0xFFFE. An unsigned multiply would instead give 2 * 255 = 0x01FE.

questions.q: CX = 0x4000 and DX = 0x0004. After `imul cx, dx`, what is CX?
questions.explain: Two-operand form: r16 = r16 * r/m16. 0x4000 * 4 = 0x10000, which needs 17 bits. Only the low 16 bits (0x0000) fit in CX, so the product is truncated.

questions.q: AX = 0x4000 and CX = 0x0004. After the one-operand `imul cx`, what are DX and AX?
questions.explain: One-operand 16-bit form: DX:AX = AX * r/m16. The 32-bit product 0x00010000 is split, with the high half (0x0001) in DX and the low half (0x0000) in AX. Nothing is lost.

questions.q: EAX = 0xF00DFACE. After `movsxd rbx, eax`, what is RBX?
questions.explain: Bit 31 of 0xF00DFACE is 1, so sign extension fills the upper 32 bits with 1s. The value stays negative.

questions.q: If the 32-bit value 0xF00DFACE is zero-extended into a 64-bit register, what is the result?
questions.explain: Zero extension fills all the new high bits with 0, even though the source's top bit is 1.

questions.q: CX = 0xFFFF. After `movzx eax, cx`, what hex value is in EAX?
questions.explain: Zero extension always fills the high 16 bits with 0, giving 0x0000FFFF (65535 as a 32-bit value).

questions.q: CX = 0xFFFF. After `movsx eax, cx`, what is EAX, and what signed value does it hold?
questions.explain: 0xFFFF is -1 as a signed 16-bit value. Sign extension copies the top bit (1) into the upper 16 bits, giving 0xFFFFFFFF, which is still -1.

questions.q: The 16-bit value 0x7ABC is sign-extended to 32 bits. What is the result?
questions.explain: Bit 15 of 0x7ABC is 0 (0x7 = 0111b), so the value is positive and sign extension fills with 0s. Here it gives the same result as zero extension.

questions.q: Like MOVSXD, there is a MOVZXD instruction for zero-extending a 32-bit value to 64 bits.
questions.explain: Only sign extension has a separate dword variant (MOVSXD). There is no MOVZXD; zero extension is always written MOVZX.

questions.q: MOVSX (without the D) sign-extends from which source sizes?
questions.explain: MOVSX takes 8- or 16-bit sources. To sign-extend a 32-bit value to 64 bits, you need MOVSXD.

questions.q: C code copies an `unsigned short` into an `unsigned int`. Which instruction fits that conversion?
questions.explain: An unsigned value's top bit isn't a sign bit, so the new upper bits must be zeros (MOVZX). A signed short going into an int would use MOVSX so that negative values stay negative.

questions.q: Zero extension fills the upper bits with 0 whether or not the source value's most significant bit is set.
questions.explain: Zero extension always fills the high bits with zeros. Only sign extension looks at the source's top bit.

questions.q: Local variables are always laid out on the stack in the order they're declared in C.
questions.explain: In ArrayLocalVariable.c (`short a; int b[6]; long long c;`), Visual Studio placed them as a, padding, c, then b. Separate locals need not follow declaration order.

questions.q: The locals are declared as `short a; int b[6]; long long c;`. In the compiled ArrayLocalVariable.c, in what order are they placed, from the lowest address up?
questions.explain: a is at [rsp], c at [rsp+8] and b at [rsp+10h]. In 4-byte rows that is a (2 bytes plus 2 undefined), 4 bytes of alignment padding, c (8 bytes), b[0] to b[5], then more padding.

questions.q: For `a = 0xbabe;` (a is a `short`), the compiler emits `mov eax, 0FFFFBABEh` and then `mov word ptr [rsp], ax`. Why the 0xFFFF?
choices: a is a signed short and 0xBABE is negative at 16 bits, so the constant was sign-extended to 32 bits; only AX (0xBABE) is stored
All four bytes 0xFFFFBABE are written into a
The short is stored on the stack as a 32-bit int
questions.explain: The top bit of 0xBABE is 1, so the compiler put the sign-extended 32-bit constant in EAX. The store is `word ptr`, so only the 2 bytes 0xBABE reach memory.

questions.q: Which instruction reads `a` (a short) so it can be stored into `b[1]` (an int)?
questions.explain: A signed 16-bit value going into a signed 32-bit int has to keep its sign, so it is MOVSX'd into ECX. `mov dword ptr [rsp+rax+10h], ecx` then stores it, making b[1] = 0xFFFFBABE.

questions.q: In the sequence `mov eax, 4` / `imul rax, rax, 1` / ... / `mov dword ptr [rsp+rax+10h], ecx`, what do 4, 1 and 10h stand for?
choices: 4 = sizeof(int), 1 = the index, 10h = where b starts relative to rsp
4 = number of elements, 1 = stride, 10h = offset of the return address
questions.explain: Unoptimized VS code finds an array element by multiplying the element size by the index with IMUL. Here 4 * 1 = byte offset 4 for b[1], which is added to the array base at [rsp+10h].

questions.q: b starts at [rsp+10h] and holds 4-byte ints. How many bytes above rsp is b[4]? (decimal)
questions.explain: 0x10 + 4*4 = 0x10 + 0x10 = 0x20 = 32. This matches `imul rcx, rcx, 4` (4*4) followed by `[rsp+rcx+10h]`.

questions.q: When main starts, RSP = 0x14FE08 (pointing at the return address). main runs `sub rsp, 38h`, and b lives at [rsp+10h]. What is the address of b[1]? (hex)
For `b[4] = b[1] + c;`, why does the compiler run `movsxd rax, dword ptr [rsp+rax+10h]` before `add rax, qword ptr [rsp+8]`?
choices: b[1] is a signed 32-bit int and c is a 64-bit long long, so b[1] is sign-extended to keep its value in the 64-bit addition
To zero the upper half of RAX before adding
Because add cannot take a memory operand
To narrow b[1] to 16 bits before adding
questions.explain: The addition is done in a 64-bit register. b[1] = 0xFFFFBABE is negative, so it must become 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFBABE to keep its value.

questions.q: c = 0x0BA1B0AB1EDB100D and b[1] = 0xFFFFBABE (signed int). What 32-bit value is stored in b[4] by `b[4] = b[1] + c;`?
questions.explain: Sign-extended, b[1] = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFBABE = -0x4542. 0x0BA1B0AB1EDB100D - 0x4542 = 0x0BA1B0AB1EDACACB. b[4] is an int, so only EAX (0x1EDACACB) is stored. You get 0x1EDBCACB if you wrongly add 0xBABE as a positive number.

questions.q: b[4] = 0x1EDACACB, and main returns `b[4]` as a short using `movzx eax, word ptr [rsp+rax+10h]`. What hex value is in EAX after that instruction?
questions.explain: The word read takes the low 2 bytes of b[4] (little-endian), 0xCACB, and MOVZX fills the rest of EAX with zeros, giving 0x0000CACB. The int is truncated to a 16-bit short.

questions.q: Struct fields must be stored in memory in the same order they are declared in C.
questions.explain: Unlike separate locals, struct fields keep their declaration order. The first field is at the lowest address and each later field is higher.

questions.q: For `typedef struct { short a; int b[6]; long long c; } mystruct_t;` in a local `foo`, which field is at the lowest stack address?
choices: It's up to the compiler, as with separate locals
questions.explain: The first declared field (the top one in the source) sits at the lowest address, followed by b and then c.

questions.q: Without any packing pragma, why are there 2 undefined bytes right after foo.a?
choices: So the int array b starts at a 4-byte-aligned offset (offset 4)
Because a short always takes 4 bytes on x86-64
To place a stack canary between fields
questions.explain: a uses offsets 0-1. Ints are aligned to 4 bytes, so b starts at offset 4, which leaves 2 bytes of padding.

questions.q: Without packing, at what byte offset from the start of foo does c begin? (decimal)
questions.explain: a (2) + padding (2) + b (6*4 = 24) = 28. The 8-byte long long is aligned to 8, so 4 bytes of struct padding are added and c starts at 32 (0x20). In the stack diagram that is 0x14FDF0 - 0x14FDD0.

questions.q: Without packing, how many bytes does mystruct_t occupy, from a through the end of c? (decimal)
questions.explain: c starts at offset 32 and is 8 bytes long, so the struct ends at offset 40 (0x28).

questions.q: What does `#pragma pack(1)` around the struct definition do?
choices: Removes the padding between struct fields, so each field starts right after the previous one
Reorders the fields to minimize padding
Aligns every field to a 1 KB boundary
Removes all padding from main's stack frame, including the 16-byte stack alignment
questions.explain: Packing to 1 squeezes the fields together with no padding between them, keeping their order. It doesn't change the padding the compiler adds around the struct in main's frame.

questions.q: With `#pragma pack(1)`, at what byte offset does c begin? (decimal)
questions.explain: a (2 bytes) + b (24 bytes) = 26 = 0x1A. That matches the `qword ptr [rsp+1Ah]` access to c.

questions.q: With `#pragma pack(1)`, how many bytes does mystruct_t occupy?
questions.explain: 2 (a) + 24 (b) + 8 (c) = 34, with no padding between fields.

questions.q: With `#pragma pack(1)`, where does b[0] fall in a stack diagram drawn in 4-byte rows?
choices: It starts at offset 2 and straddles two rows: its 2 low bytes share a row with a, and its 2 high bytes are in the next row
It starts at offset 4 in its own row
It overlaps a, since packing lets fields overlap
questions.explain: With no padding after the 2-byte a, b[0] covers offsets 2-5 and crosses a 4-byte boundary. c ends up split across three rows for the same reason.

questions.q: A struct local's assembly reads foo.a at [rsp], foo.b[i] as `dword ptr [rsp+rax+2]` and foo.c as `qword ptr [rsp+1Ah]`. Which layout does this match?
choices: Packed: b at offset 2 and c at offset 0x1A, with no padding between fields
Natural alignment: b at offset 4 and c at offset 0x20
Reordered fields: c first, then b, then a
Every field padded out to 8 bytes
questions.explain: With natural alignment the accesses would be [rsp+rax+4] and [rsp+20h]. Offsets 2 and 0x1A mean there is no padding after a or after b, which is the pack(1) layout.

questions.q: Comparing ArrayLocalVariable.c (a, b and c as separate locals) with StructLocalVariable.c (the same three as struct fields), which statements are true?
choices: The separate locals were rearranged on the stack (a, c, b)
The struct fields kept declaration order (a, b, c)
#pragma pack(1) removes the padding between the struct's fields
#pragma pack(1) also removes the padding the compiler puts around the struct in main's frame
questions.explain: Packing only changes the struct's internal layout. The packed version still had plenty of padding above the struct in main's frame, plus the 16-byte stack-alignment slot.
